title: Under Heaven, Under Ink
subtitle: Tianzhao society and visual identity
summary: Cinnabar, jade and ink; palace terraces beside factory chimneys; rank badges, paper seals that are only notices, and shrines bolted to the presses.
content:
> *"It is a notice." (A pause.) "You should still not remove it."*
> — a Tianzhao official, to a foreign visitor

Tianzhao looks like what it is: a very old civilisation that has taken in railways, factories and precision machinery without ever deciding that its past was something to be replaced. Its visual identity communicates **age**, **refinement**, **precision**, **symmetry**, **hidden complexity** and, above all, **continuity** between old and new.

This entry describes how the [Tianzhao Mandate](factions.html#tianzhao-mandate) looks and behaves. For its history and government, see [[the-tianzhao-mandate|The Tianzhao Mandate]]. For the spirits, ancestors and officials behind its paper seals, see [[ten-thousand-offices-of-heaven|The Ten Thousand Offices of Heaven]].

## Cinnabar, Jade and Ink

The Tianzhao palette is **cinnabar** red, **jade** green, ink **black**, **ivory**, muted **gold** and deep **blue**. Its materials are **lacquer**, **black iron**, **bronze**, **jade**, **porcelain**, **silk**, **paper** and, in its machinery, **ceramic** insulation.

Clouds, cranes and gates recur across Tianzhao design: on robes and rank badges, on jade and porcelain ornaments, on banners, buildings and equipment.

![The flag of the Tianzhao Mandate](data/images/tianzhao-mandate-flag-b01942c3.jpg "The Tianzhao flag: a vermilion gatehouse beneath a radiant sun, wreathed in clouds, inside a jade-green ring set with four stars, on a cinnabar field banded in black, green and gold with cloud scrolls. Gate and cloud motifs like these recur on insignia, ornaments and architecture across the Mandate.")

## Old Cities, New Machines

Tianzhao cities show their whole history at once: old ceremonial architecture, courtyards, gardens and walled administrative compounds alongside railways, factories, chimneys and modern infrastructure. The modern buildings do not replace the old ones. They are fitted into a continuous architectural tradition, often in the same colours and with the same rooflines.

![A Tianzhao city on its river](data/images/tianzhao-mandate-homeland-e16867e5.jpg "A Tianzhao river city. Notice how old and new are layered rather than separated: vermilion gate towers over the water, terraced palace compounds climbing the cliffs beside factory chimneys, a steam train crossing a stone viaduct, steamships flying the Mandate's emblem on their sails, and lanterns and pines on the terraces.")

Anyone who arrives expecting a country frozen in the past is quickly corrected. Tianzhao is not technologically stagnant. It simply does not see why becoming modern should mean forgetting who you were.

## Dress and Rank

Tianzhao clothing favours **layered robes**, **structured coats**, broad ceremonial sleeves, high collars, **rank badges** and jade or metal insignia. Industrial and field clothing adapts the older forms for practical work, rather than abandoning them. An official, a worker, a scholar, a soldier and a physician should never be mistaken for one another, and the details of a badge or sash tell those who can read them exactly who they are dealing with.

![Tianzhao clothing: commoner, diplomat, soldier and Expeditioner](data/images/tianzhao-mandate-clothing-b9528577.jpg "Four Tianzhao people. A townsperson in layered, durable, neat everyday clothes; a scholar-official in elegant layered robes with embroidered trim and rank insignia, carrying documents and seals; a soldier whose armour joins traditional forms to industrial-era practicality; and a Gate Expeditioner in field-ready layers carrying maps, tools, medicines and talismans. Note the paper seals and talismans, the lacquered accessories, the rank badges with different motifs for civil, military and regional offices, and the medicine kit that doubles as a talisman case.")

## Paper, Seals and Notices

Paper matters enormously in Tianzhao. Official notices, ritual inscriptions, seals, containment warnings, permits and ancestral records are everywhere, and they often look alike. Visitors frequently cannot tell which kind of document they are looking at, and the people who live there are not always in a hurry to explain. The overlap is real: in Tianzhao, a seal on a door may be an administrative order, a religious act and a safety warning all at once.

> **In a warehouse in Endros, a foreign visitor and a Pavilion official**
>
> The visitor pointed at the strip of red paper pasted across the lid of a crate, covered in brushed characters and stamped with a seal.
>
> "Is that a spell?"
>
> "No," said the official. "It is a notice."
>
> The visitor relaxed a little and reached for the lid.
>
> The official waited until the visitor's hand was nearly on the crate.
>
> "You should still not remove it."

## Machines and Shrines

Tianzhao machinery is built for **precision**, **balance** and **symmetry**, often with **ceramic** components, **segmented** construction and **lacquered** surfaces. It looks as though it was integrated into an old civilisation rather than imposed on it, and that is exactly the impression it is meant to give.

Factories may hold **shrines**, ritual notices and protective inscriptions alongside their safety placards, and geomancers and engineers routinely work on the same projects. To Tianzhao, neither is the superstition and neither is the science. Both are ways of managing different aspects of one world.

> **At the start of the night shift in a Tianzhao rolling mill**
>
> Before she threw the lever on the great press, the operator stepped to the small shrine bolted to the pillar beside it, lit a stick of incense, set a single cracker on the plate, and bowed.
>
> The visiting Vardic engineer watched with interest. "Does it make the press safer?"
>
> "The guard rails make the press safer," she said. "The maintenance schedule makes the press safer. This" (she nodded at the shrine) "makes sure everyone remembers that the press can kill you." She threw the lever. "That also makes it safer."

> **On a railway survey in the hills**
>
> The engineer laid the route plans on the table. The geomancer laid his compass beside them.
>
> "Your line crosses the ridge here," said the geomancer, "through the saddle where the old shrine stands. That is a bad place to cut."
>
> "It is the shortest route."
>
> "It is the shortest route, and the ground under the saddle is full of water. The village has known that for a thousand years, which is why they put the shrine there and not a house."
>
> The engineer looked at the plans for a long time. Then he picked up a pencil and moved the line half a mile east.

## The Admired Person

The culturally admired Tianzhao person **observes before acting**, **understands relationships**, **considers consequences**, **avoids unnecessary display** and prefers **the correct result to the dramatic gesture**. Restraint is a virtue; so is very dry humour.

Heroic sacrifice that could have been avoided is not much admired. It tends to be seen as **poor planning**. A victory won without a fight is admired far more than one won by spectacle.

## What Foreigners Get Wrong

Foreigners often decide that Tianzhao is mystical, stagnant or inscrutable. It is none of these. Its people are not speaking in riddles; they are being polite, and choosing their words carefully, which is not the same thing. Its technology is modern. And very little in Tianzhao is truly hidden. It is simply filed, under a category the visitor did not think to ask about.
